intro: Every country has to answer a hard question. Who gets to make the rules? In some places a king or queen decides. In others, voters choose leaders and can replace them. In still others, one person or one party holds power and no one can vote them out.

People also argue about what the rules should be. For more than 200 years, they have used two words to sort those arguments: left and right. These words began with where lawmakers sat in a French hall in 1789. Today you hear them on the news almost every day, in many countries.

In this unit you will learn where left and right came from and what they usually mean. You will compare monarchy, democracy and dictatorship. By the end, you will be able to spot the signs of a free and fair election and explain ideas from different sides fairly.
bigQuestion: How do people decide who holds power, and how can citizens tell whether that power is fair and limited?

title: Left, Right and the Kinds of Government

chapters.title: Where Left and Right Came From
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do we sort political ideas into left and right, and what does that simple picture miss?

story.title: Two Sides of a Hot Hall
story.kicker: In 1789 French lawmakers picked their seats in a crowded hall, and the way they sat gave the world two new political words.
paragraphs: It is the summer of 1789 in France. Hundreds of deputies crowd into a large hall. They have come from every part of the country. Some are priests. Some are nobles in fine coats. Most are lawyers, merchants and other commoners. The air is hot, and the arguments are hotter.

Only weeks before, these deputies did something bold. They declared that they were a National Assembly. They said they spoke for the whole French nation, not just for the king. Now they must decide a hard question. How much power should King Louis XVI keep?

One question splits the room. Should the king be able to block any law the Assembly passes? Deputies who want to protect the king's power drift to one side of the hall. They sit to the right of the Assembly's president. Deputies who want big changes gather on the other side, to his left.

At first, no one plans it. It is just easier to sit near friends and cheer together. But soon people talk about 'the right' and 'the left' as if they were teams. More than 200 years later, people around the world still use those two words. They began with where people chose to sit.
story.think: The deputies sat near people who agreed with them. How can sitting in groups make a disagreement feel bigger or smaller?

lessons.title: The Three Estates Meet
lessons.mainIdea: In 1789 the king called the Estates-General, and the commoners broke away to form a National Assembly.
reading: In May 1789, King Louis XVI of France had a problem. His government was deeply in debt. He needed new taxes. So he called a meeting that had not been held since 1614. It was called the *Estates-General*, and it met at the royal palace of Versailles.

French society was divided into three *estates*, or orders. The First Estate was the clergy, the leaders of the Catholic Church. The Second Estate was the nobility. The Third Estate was everyone else, from rich bankers to poor farmers. The Third Estate held almost all the people, but each estate had one vote as a group.

The Third Estate's deputies felt the voting was unfair. Two groups could always outvote them. On June 17, 1789, they declared themselves a National Assembly for the whole nation. Three days later, locked out of their hall, they met on a tennis court. They swore not to leave until France had a constitution.

words.d: one of the three legal orders of old French society: clergy, nobles and commoners
a meeting of deputies from all three estates, called by the French king

look.title: Deputies at the Estates-General, 1789
look.cite: Rounded figures given in standard histories, e.g., William Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (1989)
look.prompt: The Third Estate had about as many deputies as the other two together. Why did that still not help them when each estate voted as one group?

check.q: Why did King Louis XVI call the Estates-General in 1789?

check.q: Which group made up the Third Estate?

check.q: What did the Third Estate's deputies do on June 17, 1789?

lessons.title: Seats Become Sides
lessons.mainIdea: Deputies who backed the king sat on the right and those who wanted change sat on the left.
reading: By late summer 1789, the new Assembly was writing rules for France. One big fight was about the king's *veto*. A veto is the power to block a law. Should Louis XVI be able to stop any law forever? Or only delay it for a while?

Deputies who wanted a strong king, and who valued old traditions, gathered to the right of the Assembly's president. Deputies who wanted to limit the king and change France quickly gathered to his left. A noble deputy later wrote that the groups began to recognize each other by where they sat.

The seats became a kind of *political* map. You could look across the hall and guess how someone would vote. Newspapers began to write about 'the left side' and 'the right side.' In the end, the Assembly gave the king only a delaying veto. The left had won that vote.

words.d: the power to block or reject a law
having to do with government, power and public decisions

look.title: A Deputy Remembers the Seating
look.text: We began to recognize one another. Those loyal to religion and the king took seats to the right of the chair, so they could avoid the shouts and noise of the other side.
look.cite: Baron de Gauville, deputy of the nobility, memoir describing August–September 1789 (paraphrased translation)
look.prompt: Why does the Baron say his side chose the right? What does that tell you about how the sides felt about each other?

check.q: In 1789, the fight over the king's veto was about whether he could
check.why: A veto is the power to block a law, and the Assembly argued over how much of it the king should have.

check.q: Where did deputies who supported the king's power usually sit?
choices: To the right of the president
To the left of the president
check.why: The reading says supporters of a strong king gathered to the right of the president.

check.q: According to the Baron de Gauville's memoir, why did his side sit together on the right?
choices: They wanted to avoid the noise and shouts of the other side

lessons.title: How Two Words Spread
lessons.mainIdea: Left and right started as seats in France and became words for political ideas around the world.
reading: The seating habit stayed in France. In French lawmaking bodies of the 1800s, groups kept sitting left, right or in between. Reporters and voters used the labels every day. The words stopped meaning a place in a room. They started to mean a set of ideas.

Other countries borrowed the words. Many parliaments in Europe sit in a half circle, like the French hall. Members often sit in blocks from left to right. Some other parliaments, like Britain's House of Commons, face each other in two rows instead. Yet people there still talk about left and right. The words spread through newspapers, books and later radio and television.

Today you can hear these words in Mexico, India, Japan, Germany and the United States. This shows how an idea from one place can become part of a *global* way of talking. But as the words traveled, their meanings shifted. You will see why that matters later in this chapter.

words.d: an elected body of lawmakers, found in many countries
having to do with the whole world

look.title: Two Room Shapes
look.text: Picture two rooms. In the first, lawmakers sit in a half circle facing the speaker, and each party fills a wedge from left to right. In the second, two long rows of benches face each other across an aisle, one side for the government and one for the opposition.
look.prompt: Which room makes it easier to see a 'middle'? Which room makes politics look like two teams? Explain your thinking.

check.q: Over time, what did the words 'left' and 'right' come to mean?
choices: Only a place in a French hall

check.why: The reading says the words stopped meaning a place in a room and started to mean a set of ideas.

check.q: How is Britain's House of Commons different from many European parliaments?

check.q: Which statement best matches the lesson?

The words are used only in France

check.why: The lesson says the words traveled to many countries and their meanings shifted along the way.

sections.title: What Left and Right Often Mean

lessons.title: The Left: Equality and Change
lessons.mainIdea: People on the left usually stress equality and are more open to changing how society works.
reading: Think of the deputies on the left in 1789. They wanted to end special privileges for nobles and clergy. In August 1789 the Assembly passed the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its first article said people are born free and equal in rights.

Since then, the *left* has usually stressed *equality*. That can mean equal rights under the law. It can also mean closing gaps between rich and poor. People on the left are often more willing to change old ways, and to use government to help people who have less.

Supporters say the left has pushed for many things people now take for granted, such as wider voting rights and limits on child labor. Critics say some left ideas cost too much, give government too much power, or change things too fast. Both sides of that debate are part of the story.

words.d: the side of politics that usually stresses equality and change
the idea that people should have the same rights or a fair share

look.title: Declaration of the Rights of Man, Article 1
look.text: Men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Social distinctions may be founded only upon the general good.
look.cite: National Assembly of France, Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, 1789 (standard English translation)
look.prompt: Which old French idea does this sentence reject? Use the words 'estates' or 'privileges' in your answer.

check.q: What does the left usually stress?
check.why: The lesson says the left has usually stressed equality and openness to change.

check.q: Article 1 of the 1789 Declaration says people are born
check.why: The Declaration says men are born and remain free and equal in rights.

check.q: Which is a criticism of some left ideas named in the lesson?
choices: They can give government too much power
check.why: The lesson says critics worry some left ideas give government too much power or cost too much.

lessons.title: The Right: Tradition, Order and Liberty
lessons.mainIdea: People on the right usually stress tradition and order, and often want liberty from too much government.
reading: Now think of the deputies on the right in 1789. They wanted to keep the king, the Church and old customs. They feared that tearing down everything at once would bring chaos. In 1790 a British writer, Edmund Burke, warned that the French Revolution was moving too fast.

Since then, the *right* has usually stressed *tradition* and order. Tradition means customs passed down from earlier generations, like family, faith and old institutions. Many on the right, especially in the United States, also stress liberty from government: lower taxes, free markets and more choices left to families.

Supporters say the right protects what has been tested by time and guards people's freedom. Critics say some right ideas protect unfair old ways or leave people with less on their own. Just like the left, the right is a family of ideas, not one single view.

words.d: the side of politics that usually stresses tradition, order and liberty from government
customs and beliefs passed down from earlier generations

look.title: Burke on Change
look.text: A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
look.cite: Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, 1790
look.prompt: Burke valued tradition, yet he says a state needs some change. What kind of change do you think he meant: fast or slow? Why?

check.q: What does 'tradition' mean in this lesson?
choices: Customs passed down from earlier generations
check.why: Tradition means customs and beliefs passed down from earlier generations.

check.q: What did Edmund Burke warn about in 1790?
choices: The French king was too weak to rule
The French Revolution was moving too fast
check.why: The lesson says Burke warned that the Revolution was moving too fast.

check.q: Burke wrote that a state 'without the means of some change' cannot
check.why: He said such a state is without the means of its conservation, meaning it cannot keep itself going.

lessons.title: Meanings Change by Place and Time
lessons.mainIdea: Left and right do not mean exactly the same thing in every country or every era.
reading: In 1789, being on the right meant supporting a king. Today, almost no one on the right in the United States wants a king. The labels stayed, but the ideas under them moved. That is the first reason to use these words with care.

The second reason is place. In the United States, the right often stresses free markets and small government. In some European countries, parties on the right have supported a large welfare system for health care. After the Soviet Union ended in 1991, some reporters called Russia's old Communist hardliners 'conservatives,' because they wanted to keep the old system.

So left and right are *relative* words. They describe a position compared with others in the same country at the same time. Before you decide what a label means, ask two questions. Where is this? And when is this?

words.d: judged by comparing with something else, not fixed
a period of time in history

look.title: Same Word, Different Meaning
look.text: A reporter in 1789 Paris writes, 'The right defends the king.' A reporter in 1991 Moscow writes, 'The conservatives want to keep the Communist system.' A student in 2020s Chicago hears, 'The right wants lower taxes.'
look.prompt: What does each writer mean by the right or conservative side? What do the three meanings have in common, if anything?

check.q: Why did some reporters call Russia's old Communist hardliners 'conservatives' after 1991?
choices: They wanted to move to the United States
They wanted to keep the old system
check.why: Conservative can mean wanting to keep the existing system, which for them was Communism.

check.q: In this lesson, 'relative' means
check.why: Left and right are relative: they describe a position compared with others in the same place and time.

check.q: Which two questions does the lesson say to ask before deciding what a label means?
choices: Who is richest? Who is oldest?
Where is this? When is this?
How loud is it? How long is it?
Who sat first? Who spoke last?
check.why: The lesson says to ask where and when, because meanings change by place and time.

sections.title: The Middle and the Limits of a Line

lessons.title: The Center
lessons.mainIdea: The center is the middle ground, where people mix ideas from left and right.
reading: Picture the French hall again. Not every deputy sat far left or far right. Some sat in the middle. They agreed with the left on some things and with the right on others. People still call this middle the *center*, and those who stand there are often called *moderates*.

A moderate voter might want to keep old traditions and also support some new programs. She might like lower taxes but also want strong public schools. Many voters in many countries describe themselves this way. Centrist parties often try to build deals between larger groups.

Supporters say the center helps a country stay calm and find compromise. A compromise is a deal where each side gives up something. Critics say the center can avoid hard choices or move too slowly on real problems. Those who sit far from the center, on either side, are often called the 'far left' and the 'far right.'

words.d: the middle of the political spectrum, mixing ideas from left and right
a person whose views are not extreme and who often seeks compromise
a deal in which each side gives up something to reach agreement

look.title: Three Neighbors
look.text: Ana wants the town to build a new park and raise taxes to pay for it. Ben wants no new taxes and no new park. Carla wants the park but paid for by cutting another program instead of raising taxes.
look.prompt: Who is closest to the center here? What compromise could all three accept?

check.q: What is a moderate?
choices: Someone who always votes with the far left
Someone whose views are not extreme and who often seeks compromise
check.why: The lesson defines a moderate as someone whose views are not extreme and who seeks compromise.

check.q: In the 'Three Neighbors' example, who takes a middle position?
check.why: Carla wants the park like Ana but no new tax like Ben, so she mixes both views.

check.q: What is one criticism of the center named in the lesson?
choices: It can avoid hard choices or move too slowly
check.why: Critics say the center can avoid hard choices or move too slowly on real problems.

lessons.title: A Line Is a Model
lessons.mainIdea: The left-right line is a simple model that helps us sort ideas, but it leaves a lot out.
reading: A map of Chicago's trains does not show every street. It leaves things out so you can find your way. Scientists and teachers call a simple picture like this a *model*. A model helps us think, but it is never the whole truth.

The left-right line is a model of politics. It is sometimes called the political *spectrum*, like the spread of colors in a rainbow. It puts ideas in one row, from far left through the center to far right. That makes it quick to compare parties and people.

But one line hides a lot. A person can want lower taxes and also want big changes to schools. Another can love old traditions and also want more help for poor families. Real people often do not fit one spot. When the line does not fit, the problem may be the model, not the person.

words.d: a simple picture or tool that helps explain something complicated
a range of positions spread out in order, like colors in a rainbow

look.title: Where Would You Put Her?
look.text: Maria runs a small bakery. She wants lower taxes on small businesses. She also wants the city to spend more on buses so her workers can get to work. She goes to church every Sunday and cares a lot about family traditions.
look.prompt: Try to place Maria on one line from left to right. What made it hard? What would you need to show her views more fully?

check.q: Why is a train map a good example of a model?
choices: It shows every street and building
It leaves things out so you can find your way
It is drawn by the government
check.why: The lesson says a model is a simple picture that leaves things out to help us think.

check.q: The political spectrum is compared to
check.why: A spectrum is a range spread out in order, like colors in a rainbow.

check.q: According to the lesson, if a person does not fit one spot on the line, the problem may be
check.why: The lesson says when the line does not fit, the problem may be the model, not the person.

lessons.title: Two Lines Instead of One
lessons.mainIdea: Some thinkers add a second line to show views about personal freedom as well as money.
reading: Because one line leaves so much out, some thinkers draw two. In the late 1960s and early 1970s, an American named David Nolan drew a well-known chart. One line shows views on economic freedom, such as taxes and business rules. The other shows views on personal freedom, such as speech and private choices.

Other scholars use a line for economics, left to right, and a second line from *authoritarian* to libertarian. Authoritarian means wanting strong control by the government over people's lives. Libertarian means wanting government to do as little as possible.

A grid with two lines can show things one line cannot. Two dictators, one on the far left and one on the far right, may sit far apart on the money line. Yet both sit near the authoritarian end, because both crush free speech. You will study them in the next chapter.

words.d: wanting strong government control over people's lives and little freedom to disagree
wanting government to do as little as possible and leave choices to individuals

look.title: Building a Grid
look.text: Draw a plus sign. The line across runs from economic left to economic right. The line up and down runs from authoritarian at the top to libertarian at the bottom. Now picture a leader who owns all factories through the state and jails critics, and another who leaves business alone but also jails critics.
look.prompt: Where would each leader go on your grid? How does the second line show something the first line hides?

check.q: What does 'authoritarian' mean?
choices: Wanting strong government control and little freedom to disagree
Wanting government to do as little as possible
Wanting to move to the center
check.why: Authoritarian means wanting strong government control over people's lives.

check.q: What did David Nolan's chart add to the one-line model?
choices: A second line for personal freedom
check.why: Nolan's chart shows economic freedom on one line and personal freedom on another.

check.q: Why might two dictators from the far left and far right sit near each other on a two-line grid?
choices: They had the same tax rates
They lived in the same country

check.why: The second line measures control over people's lives, and both kinds of dictators used heavy control.

lessons.title: Using the Labels Fairly
lessons.mainIdea: Use left and right to understand ideas, not to judge or stereotype people.
reading: Labels can help. If a newspaper says a party is center-right, you get a quick idea of its views. But labels can also hurt. If you hear someone is 'on the left' or 'on the right,' you might guess what they believe about everything. That guess is often wrong.

A *stereotype* is a fixed idea that all people in a group are the same. Political stereotypes are common. They can make people stop listening to each other. Good citizens ask questions first. What do you think about this issue, and why?

Here is a helpful habit. When you hear a label, look for the actual idea underneath. Ask what the person wants, and what reasons they give. Describe the idea the way its supporters would, and then the way its critics would. That is how historians and careful citizens use these words.

words.d: a fixed idea that all people in a group are the same
a short word or name used to sort people or ideas

check.q: In 'Two Ways to Start a Talk,' what does Student B do well?

check.q: What habit does the lesson recommend when you hear a political label?

chapters.title: Monarchy, Democracy and Dictatorship
chapters.bigQuestion: Who should hold power, and how can people tell whether they really choose their leaders?

story.title: Two Ballots on the Same Day
story.kicker: Two imagined countries vote on the same Sunday, and the ballots tell very different stories.
paragraphs: Imagine two countries holding elections on the same Sunday. In the first country, a woman named Lena walks to a school gym. She shows her name to a volunteer. She takes a paper ballot into a small booth with a curtain. Four names are printed on it, from four different parties.

Lena has watched the candidates argue on television for weeks. Newspapers have criticized every one of them. She marks her choice in private and drops the ballot in a box. That night, workers from several parties watch as the votes are counted. The leader in office loses, and she gives a speech thanking the winner.

In the second country, a man named Arman also goes to vote. His ballot has only one name. Next to it is a single box. There is a booth, but an official stands close by and watches who uses it. Posters of the one candidate cover the walls. No newspaper has printed a word against him.

The next day, the government announces that the candidate won almost every vote. Both countries held an election. Both can say that the people voted. But only one of them gave people a real choice. This chapter is about how to tell the difference.
story.think: Both countries held an election. What three details from the story show which election gave people a real choice?

lessons.title: Absolute Monarchy
lessons.mainIdea: In an absolute monarchy, one king or queen holds nearly all power and answers to no elected body.
reading: King Louis XIV of France ruled from 1643 to 1715, one of the longest reigns in European history. He built a huge palace at Versailles and made nobles live near him so he could watch them. He made war, set taxes and named officials largely as he chose.

This kind of government is called an *absolute monarchy*. A *monarch* is a king or queen who usually inherits the throne from a parent. In an absolute monarchy, the monarch's word is law. Many kings of that time said their right to rule came from God. This idea is called the divine right of kings.

Supporters said one strong ruler brought order and unity after years of civil war. Critics said no single person should have so much power, because no one could stop a ruler who made bad choices. A few countries today, such as Saudi Arabia, are still described as absolute monarchies.

words.d: a king or queen, who usually inherits the throne
a government in which the monarch holds nearly all power
the belief that a monarch's power comes from God

lessons.title: Constitutional Monarchy
lessons.mainIdea: In a constitutional monarchy, the king or queen is head of state, but elected lawmakers make the laws.
reading: Britain went a different way. After years of struggle between kings and Parliament, the English Bill of Rights of 1689 limited the monarch. The king could not raise taxes or keep an army in peacetime without Parliament's consent. Over the next centuries, real power moved to elected lawmakers.

Today the United Kingdom is a *constitutional monarchy*. A *constitution* is the set of basic rules for a government. The king is the head of state and has an important role at public events. But the prime minister and Parliament make decisions, and the monarch stays out of party politics.

Japan, Spain, Sweden and Norway are also constitutional monarchies. Supporters say a monarch above politics can unite a country and link it to its history. Critics say no one should hold a public position just because of who their parents were. People in these countries still debate it.

words.d: the set of basic rules that says how a government works and what it may do
a government with a monarch whose powers are limited by a constitution and elected lawmakers

lessons.title: Monarchs in Today's World
lessons.mainIdea: Only a small share of countries still have a monarch, and most of those monarchs have limited power.
reading: The United Nations has 193 member countries. Only about 43 of them have a monarch as head of state. That count includes 15 countries, such as Canada, Australia and Jamaica, that share King Charles III of the United Kingdom as their king.

Most of today's monarchies are constitutional. Their kings, queens and emperors open parliaments, greet visitors and stand for national unity. A smaller number, mostly in the Middle East, still give the monarch real control over government.
Most countries have no monarch at all. Many of them are *republics*. In a republic, the head of state is chosen, not born into the job. You will learn more about republics in the next section.

words.d: the person who officially stands for a country, such as a monarch or president
a country whose head of state is chosen rather than inheriting the position

lessons.title: Direct Democracy
lessons.mainIdea: In a direct democracy, citizens vote on laws themselves instead of choosing others to do it.
reading: Around 500 BCE, the Greek city of Athens began one of the first *democracies*. The word comes from Greek words meaning 'the people rule.' Male citizens met on a hillside called the Pnyx. Thousands at a time listened to speeches and voted by raising their hands.

This is called *direct democracy*, because citizens decide laws themselves. But Athens left many people out. Women, enslaved people and foreigners living in the city could not vote. Only a minority of the people who lived there took part.

Direct democracy still exists in small places. In two Swiss cantons, or states, citizens meet outdoors once a year and vote by raising their hands. Many U.S. states, including Illinois, also let voters decide some questions directly on the ballot. Supporters say this is the purest form of self-rule. Critics say it is hard to run a big country this way.

words.d: government in which the people hold power, usually by voting
a democracy in which citizens vote on laws themselves
a full member of a country or city, with rights and duties

lessons.title: Representatives and Republics
lessons.mainIdea: In a representative democracy, people elect lawmakers to make decisions for them.
reading: The United States has more than 330 million people. They cannot all meet on a hill. So they elect *representatives*, people chosen to make laws for them. This is called representative democracy. Illinois voters, for example, elect members of the Illinois General Assembly in Springfield and members of Congress in Washington, D.C.

The United States is also a republic, because its president is elected, not born into power. France, Mexico and India are republics too. Each has an elected leader and elected lawmakers, though their systems differ in the details.

Most democracies today are representative. Supporters say representatives can study hard issues full time. Critics say representatives may drift away from what voters want. That is why regular elections matter: voters can keep a representative or replace one.

words.d: a person elected to make decisions and laws for a group of people
a democracy in which people elect lawmakers to decide for them

lessons.title: Checks and Balances
lessons.mainIdea: Checks and balances split power so that no one part of government can rule alone.
reading: Suppose Congress passes a law. The president can *veto* it, or refuse to sign it. Congress can still override the veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses. Later, the courts can decide whether the law follows the Constitution.

This system is called *checks and balances*. Power is split among three branches. The legislative branch makes laws. The executive branch carries them out. The judicial branch, the courts, decides what laws mean. Each branch can limit, or check, the others.

James Madison, one of the writers of the U.S. Constitution, explained the idea in 1788. People who hold power might misuse it, so power must be set against power. Many democracies divide power in some way. Critics note that checks can also make government slow, and some people see that slowness as a benefit.

words.d: a system in which each branch of government can limit the others
one of the main parts of a government: legislative, executive or judicial
the power to reject a law

look.title: Madison on Power
look.text: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition. If men were angels, no government would be necessary.
look.prompt: What does Madison think about people who hold power? How do checks and balances follow from that idea?

check.why: The legislative branch, Congress, makes laws.

check.why: The reading says Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both houses.

check.q: Madison wrote, 'If men were angels, no government would be necessary.' What is his point?
choices: People are imperfect, so power needs limits
check.why: Madison meant that because people can misuse power, government must set power against power.

lessons.title: Free and Fair Elections
lessons.mainIdea: A free and fair election gives real choices, a secret vote, an honest count and a peaceful handover.
reading: Think back to Lena and Arman in the story. Both voted. But only Lena's vote could change who led her country. What made the difference? Political scientists look for a few clear signs.

First, there are real choices: more than one party can run and campaign. Second, the vote is a *secret ballot*, so no one can punish you for your choice. Third, the press is free to criticize any candidate. Fourth, the count is honest and watched by different sides.

The last sign is the most telling. A leader who loses must accept it and hand over power peacefully. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted by the United Nations in 1948, says government should rest on the will of the people, shown in genuine elections.

words.d: a way of voting in private so no one knows or can punish your choice
an election with real choices, a secret vote, a free press and an honest count

look.title: Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21
look.text: The will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government; this will shall be expressed in periodic and genuine elections which shall be by universal and equal suffrage and shall be held by secret vote or by equivalent free voting procedures.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 21(3), 1948
look.prompt: Find two words in this passage that describe a fair election. Which one did Arman's election fail?

choices: It lets the government know your vote

check.why: A secret ballot keeps your choice private so no one can punish you.

check.q: Which sign does the lesson call the most telling?
choices: A high number of votes for one person
A losing leader handing over power peacefully
check.why: The lesson says the most telling sign is that a losing leader accepts it and hands over power.

check.q: According to Article 21, what should be the basis of a government's authority?
check.why: Article 21 says the will of the people shall be the basis of the authority of government.

lessons.title: One-Party States
lessons.mainIdea: In a one-party state, only one party may hold power, and other parties are banned or powerless.
reading: In the Soviet Union, from its early years until 1990, only the Communist Party was allowed to rule. Elections were held, but usually with one approved candidate for each seat. This is called a *one-party state*.

China today is a one-party state led by the Chinese Communist Party. Cuba, Vietnam and North Korea are also run by a single ruling party. Some of these states allow small, loyal parties to exist, but none of them may challenge the ruling party for power.

Supporters in these countries have argued that one party can plan for the long term and keep the nation united. Critics say that without rivals, a free press or fair votes, citizens cannot remove leaders who fail or abuse power. Human rights groups report jailing of critics in many one-party states.

words.d: a country where only one political party is allowed to hold power
an organized group that shares ideas and tries to win elections or power

check.q: What do critics say is the main problem with one-party states?

check.why: Without rivals or fair votes, citizens have no way to replace leaders.

lessons.title: Military Rule
lessons.mainIdea: Military rule happens when the armed forces take over and govern a country.
reading: On September 11, 1973, tanks rolled through Santiago, Chile. The army, led by General Augusto Pinochet, overthrew the elected president, Salvador Allende. This kind of sudden, forceful takeover is called a *coup*.

Pinochet's military government ruled until 1990. It closed Congress, banned parties and arrested thousands of opponents. Many were tortured or killed. Its supporters said it saved Chile from chaos and built a stronger economy. Chile returned to democracy after voters rejected Pinochet in a 1988 vote.

Chile is one example among many. Argentina, Greece, Myanmar and Nigeria have all had periods of *military rule*. Generals often promise order and quick fixes. Critics note that armies are trained to give orders, not to listen to voters, and that military rulers often hold on to power.

words.d: a sudden, often violent takeover of a government by a small group, often the army
government run by the armed forces instead of elected leaders

look.title: Two Promises

choices: A sudden takeover of a government, often by the army

lessons.title: Dictators of the 1900s
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1900s, dictators on both the far left and the far right took total control and caused enormous suffering.
reading: A *dictator* is a ruler who holds total power and cannot be removed by fair votes. The 1900s saw some of the most destructive dictators in history. Some came from the far left. Others came from the far right. You will study them in depth in later grades.

On the far left, Joseph Stalin ruled the Soviet Union from the late 1920s until 1953. Millions died in his labor camps, called the Gulag, and in famines and purges. Mao Zedong ruled China from 1949 to 1976. Tens of millions died in the famine of his Great Leap Forward.

On the far right, Benito Mussolini ruled Italy from 1922 to 1943. Adolf Hitler ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945. His Nazi government murdered about six million Jews in the Holocaust, along with millions of others. Their ideas differed, but all four crushed free speech, banned rivals and used terror. This is why the two-line grid places them all near the authoritarian end.

words.d: a ruler with total power who cannot be removed by fair votes
the Nazi murder of about six million Jews, along with millions of others, during World War II
